1.open: What is a story or a name from your family's history that you find interesting, funny or a little embarrassing?
questions: Matthew opens with a list of names, calling Jesus "the son of David, the son of Abraham" (v. 1). Why might he start with a family history instead of a story? What does it tell us about where Jesus fits in God's plan?

Four women appear in the list: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and Bathsheba, who is called only "Uriah's wife" (v. 6). Scholars debate why Matthew includes them. What do you notice about them, and what might their presence say to people with messy or outsider stories?
Most families have a chapter they would rather leave out. How does it feel to know that Jesus' own family tree has some of those?

Joseph is called "a righteous man" who was "unwilling to disgrace her publicly" (v. 19). What does being righteous look like in how he handles a painful situation? How is it different from what you might expect?
The angel tells Joseph, "do not be afraid to embrace Mary as your wife" (v. 20). When have you faced something unexpected that you did not ask for and did not know how to handle?
Verse 21 says Jesus "will save His people from their sins." What does that tell us about why he came? How does it sit with you, whether it feels like good news, confusing, or hard to take in?
Matthew explains that Immanuel means "God with us" (v. 23). Some days that feels easy to believe and some days it does not. Where are you today, honestly?
1.life: Read the book of Ruth this week. It is only four short chapters. Notice how God works through someone from outside Israel, and think about what it says about who belongs in his story.
1.prayer: Thank God that he came to be "God with us" in real families and real messes. Ask for the trust Joseph showed when life does not go as planned.
1.tip: The virgin birth may draw questions or disagreement, since Christians understand it in different ways. Name that plainly, avoid turning the night into a debate, and bring people back to what Matthew says it means: Jesus came from God to be with us and to save.

2.open: Have you ever traveled a long way, or gone out of your way, to see or do something that mattered to you? What made it worth the trip?
questions: The Magi say, "We saw His star in the east and have come to worship Him" (v. 2). They were outsiders who traveled far for this. What does it say to you that the first people to come looking for Jesus were not Jewish?
Verse 3 says Herod "was disturbed, and all Jerusalem with him." Why might a newborn king frighten some people while others rejoice? What do you think was at stake for them?
The chief priests and scribes knew exactly where the Christ would be born (vv. 4-6), but only the Magi went to find him. Why can someone know a lot about God and still not go looking for him?
Herod says he wants to "worship Him" (v. 8), but he means to kill him. When have you seen religious words used to cover something selfish or harmful?

When the Magi found the Child, "they fell down and worshiped Him" and "presented Him with gifts" (v. 11). What would it look like for you to bring Jesus something of real value, and what might hold you back?
Joseph is warned in dreams and acts quickly, taking the family away "by night" (v. 14). The family becomes refugees. What does it mean to you that God's Son began life running from danger?

Matthew recalls "Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted" (v. 18). The chapter gives no neat answer to the killing of the Bethlehem boys. How do you want to respond when a passage leaves grief unresolved? If you are not sure what to make of it, or of God in the face of suffering, you can say so.
Jesus ends up in Nazareth, a small and overlooked village (v. 23). What does it say about God that his Son grew up somewhere so ordinary?
2.life: The Magi made a long trip to honor Jesus. This week, set aside one stretch of time you would normally spend on something else, and give it to Jesus. Pray, read a Gospel, or sit quietly. Then tell someone in the group how it went.
2.prayer: Thank God for welcoming people from far away, and for coming near to us in a child. Ask for a heart that seeks Jesus rather than fears him. Remember anyone in the group who is grieving or afraid right now.
2.tip: Verses 16 to 18 are painful, and someone may ask why God saved Jesus but not the other children. Do not rush to explain it. Say plainly that the text leaves the grief open, let people be sad, and note that Christians also differ on whether the star and the killings are straightforward history or a story shaped to echo Israel's scriptures. Keep the focus on what the chapter shows about Herod, the Magi and Jesus.

3.open: What is the strangest or most memorable outfit or food you have ever seen someone commit to?
questions: John preaches, "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near" (v. 2). In your own words, what does it mean to repent, and why does John link it to the kingdom arriving?
People came to John "confessing their sins" (v. 6). Why do you think so many were willing to admit their wrongs in public? What makes honest confession hard today?
John tells the religious leaders to "produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance" (v. 8). What might that kind of fruit look like in ordinary life, at home, at work or in the neighborhood?

John warns, "We have Abraham as our father" will not protect anyone (v. 9). What are some things people lean on today to feel safe with God, like family background, church attendance or being a decent person?

John says the one coming will baptize "with the Holy Spirit and with fire" (v. 11), and he describes wheat and chaff in verse 12. Some readers hear that mainly as judgment and others also as cleansing. How do you hear it, and what stirs up in you?

John says, "I need to be baptized by You, and do You come to me?" (v. 14). Christians differ on why Jesus chose to be baptized. What do you make of Jesus standing in line with people who were confessing their sins?
The voice from heaven says, "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!" (v. 17). This comes before Jesus has taught or healed anyone. What does it say to you that love is spoken first?
If you are honest, is it easier right now to picture God as the one with the axe in verse 10 or the one speaking in verse 17? What shapes that, and what would you like to be true?
3.life: John asked for fruit that fits a changed heart. This week, choose one small, specific thing you have been putting off, such as an apology, a phone call or a habit, and do it. Then thank God that his welcome does not depend on how well you do.
3.prayer: Ask God to show you one honest thing to turn from, and to help you hear his voice of love as clearly as his call to change. Pray for anyone in the group who feels far from him.
3.tip: Verses 7 to 12 are sharp, and some people will only hear fear while others will skip past the warning. Name both gently: John is serious about change, and the chapter ends with the Father's delight in his Son. Invite quiet or doubting members to say what they honestly feel about judgment, and do not rush to settle it.

4.open: When you were younger, what was the hardest thing to wait for, and did you ever give in and take a shortcut?
questions: The Spirit "led" Jesus into the wilderness to be tempted (v. 1). How does it land with you that testing can come right after a high moment like his baptism?
The devil begins twice with "If You are the Son of God" (vv. 3, 6). Why might doubt about who we are be such a strong place to be tested?

Jesus answers, "Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God" (v. 4). What does it look like for you to depend on God and not only on what you can provide for yourself?
The devil quotes Scripture in verse 6, and Jesus answers with another verse (v. 7). How can we tell when a verse is being used well and when it is being twisted?
In the third test the devil offers "all the kingdoms of the world and their glory" for worship (vv. 8, 9). What shortcuts to success, comfort or control are offered to people today?
Jesus begins preaching, "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near" (v. 17). What do you think it means to turn toward God's rule, and what makes that hard or appealing to you?

Peter and Andrew "at once" left their nets, and James and John left their boat and their father (vv. 20, 22). If you are honest, what holds you back from following quickly, and what questions would you want to ask first?
Verses 23 to 25 show Jesus teaching, healing and drawing large crowds. If you were in that crowd, what would you be hoping to bring to him?
4.life: This week, when you feel pulled toward a shortcut, whether it is a small lie, a quick fix or something that puts you first, pause and ask what it would look like to trust God instead. Write down one word or phrase from Scripture to hold onto, as Jesus did.
4.prayer: Thank God that Jesus faced real testing and stayed faithful for us. Ask for help to trust him in the places where you feel hungry, tempted or unsure.
4.tip: Some will wonder whether the temptations were physical events or a vision or inner struggle, and Christians read it both ways. Say so in a sentence, then steer back to what Jesus says and does. Also watch for people who feel guilty about being tempted at all; point out that Jesus was tempted too, and that being tempted is not the same as failing.

5.open: Who is someone who made a real difference in your life without ever making a fuss about it?
questions: Jesus begins with "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (v. 3). Who does he say is fortunate here, and why might that surprise the crowd on the hillside?
Some readers take the Beatitudes as qualities to aim for, and others hear them as good news for people already in hard places. Which way do they land on you right now, and why?
Verse 4 says "Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted." If you are in a season where comfort feels far off, or where you doubt it will come, what would you honestly say about that?
Jesus says, "You are the light of the world" and wants people to "glorify your Father in heaven" (vv. 14, 16). What does it look like to be seen doing good without trying to be admired for it?

In verses 21 to 24 Jesus says to leave your gift at the altar and "first go and be reconciled to your brother." Why do you think he puts making things right ahead of worship? Is there a relationship that comes to mind?

Jesus says "I tell you" again and again, taking commands about murder, adultery and oaths down to anger, lust and plain honesty (vv. 22, 28, 37). What is he showing us about what God cares about beneath the outward rules?

Christians read verses 38 to 42 differently. Some take them as a literal way of life, and others as ruling out personal revenge while still allowing courts and self defense. Where do you find this hard, and why?
Verse 44 says, "Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you." What might that look like in practice for someone who has truly wronged you, and what makes it so difficult?
5.life: Pick one person who has hurt or irritated you. This week, pray for them by name each day, and look for one small, quiet act of kindness toward them if it is safe and wise to do so.
5.prayer: Thank God that he sends his sun and rain on the good and the bad alike. Ask for a heart that grows in love, and for help where forgiveness feels out of reach.
5.tip: Verses 27 to 32 on lust and divorce can touch real pain in the room. Don't try to settle the debates. Say plainly that Christians differ, keep the focus on Jesus' concern for the heart and for the vulnerable, and let anyone pass on a question without comment.

6.open: What is a small kindness someone did for you that they never mentioned or took credit for?
questions: Jesus says, "Be careful not to perform your righteous acts before men to be seen by them" (v. 1). Why is it so easy to want an audience for the good we do, even in small ways?
Verse 4 says, "your giving may be in secret." What do you think Jesus wants for the giver here, and not only for the person receiving?

Verse 6 says to "go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father, who is unseen." Where and when do you find it easiest to pray honestly? If prayer feels awkward or empty for you right now, what makes it that way?
Jesus says God "knows what you need before you ask Him" (v. 8), and then teaches us to ask anyway. Why might God want us to pray if He already knows?
In the Lord's Prayer we ask, "Give us this day our daily bread" (v. 11). What would change in your week if you prayed that sincerely, as someone who depends on God for today?
Verses 14 and 15 connect God's forgiveness to our forgiving others. How do you hear those words: as a warning, a challenge, or something else? Who comes to mind when you think of forgiving?
Jesus says, "where your treasure is, there your heart will be also" (v. 21). Looking at your calendar and bank account, what do they say about where your heart is going?

Jesus says, "do not worry about your life" (v. 25), and then points to the birds and the lilies. What do you actually worry about most, and what would it look like to bring that to God without pretending the worry isn't real?
6.life: Pick one good thing to do quietly this week, such as a gift, a note, or an act of help, and tell no one about it. Then each night, spend two minutes telling God one thing you are worried about.
6.prayer: Thank God that He sees what is done in secret and knows what you need. Ask Him to loosen the grip of worry and the need to be noticed, and to teach you to pray the Lord's Prayer from the heart.
6.tip: Verses 14 and 15 and the word "reward" can leave people anxious or confused, especially anyone who has been hurt badly. Christians read the reward language differently: some see real rewards from God for sincere good deeds, others stress that God's favor is a gift we cannot earn. Say that plainly, don't force an answer, and make clear that forgiving is often a slow process, not a switch. Keep returning to the chapter's heart: living for God, not for an audience.

7.open: Who is someone who gave you good advice at the right time, and what did they say?
questions: Jesus says, "Do not judge, or you will be judged" (v. 1). What do you think he is warning against, and what is he not warning against?
He asks, "Why do you look at the speck in your brother's eye but fail to notice the beam in your own eye?" (v. 3). Why is it so much easier to see flaws in other people than in ourselves?

Verse 6 says not to "throw your pearls before swine." Interpreters are not sure exactly who Jesus means, but many read it as a call for good sense about who is ready to listen. How might that balance the verses before it?

Jesus says, "Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you" (v. 7). What has asking God for something been like for you lately? If it has been hard or quiet, you can say so honestly.
In verses 9 to 11 Jesus compares God to a parent who gives good gifts, not a stone or a snake. What picture of God do you tend to carry, and where did it come from?
Verse 12 says, "In everything, then, do to others as you would have them do to you." Where would that change something in your week, at home, at work or online?

Jesus says "only a few find" the narrow way (v. 14), and that some who say "Lord, Lord" will hear "I never knew you" (vv. 21 to 23). Christians differ on how these demands fit with being saved by grace through faith. How do these words land with you: as a warning, an invitation, or something else?
Jesus ends with a house on rock and a house on sand (vv. 24 to 27). What is one thing you have heard from Jesus that is easier to agree with than to act on?
7.life: Pick one small thing from this chapter to actually do this week. It might be holding back a harsh word about someone, praying for something you have been afraid to ask for, or treating one person the way you would want to be treated.
7.prayer: Ask God to help you see yourself honestly and others kindly. Thank him that he gives good things to those who ask, and ask for help to build your life on what Jesus says.
7.tip: Verse 1 is often used to shut down any hard conversation, and verses 21 to 23 can leave sincere people anxious about whether they are really saved. Gently note that Jesus himself goes on to talk about discerning fruit (vv. 15 to 20), and that he contrasts words with a life lived toward God, not a perfect record. Remind the group that Christians read how grace and obedience fit together in different ways, and make room for anyone who feels unsettled.

8.open: Who is someone you would trust to help you in a crisis, and what makes you trust them?
questions: The man with leprosy says, "Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean" (v. 2). Is it harder for you to believe God is able to help, or that he is willing? Why?

Jesus "reached out His hand and touched the man" (v. 3). Under the law, touching a person like this was forbidden. What does that touch tell you about how Jesus treats people others keep at a distance?
The centurion says, "just say the word, and my servant will be healed" (v. 8). He was a Roman officer and not Jewish. Why do you think Jesus was so struck by his faith (v. 10)?

In verses 11 and 12 Jesus says many will come "from the east and the west" to the feast, while some who expected a place will be left out. Who might the first listeners have been surprised to see at that table?
Matthew says Jesus "took up our infirmities and carried our diseases" (v. 17). What does it mean to you that Jesus carries pain and not only fixes it?
Jesus tells one eager follower, "the Son of Man has no place to lay His head" (v. 20). What do you think following Jesus costs, and where do you feel that cost most?
The disciples cry out, "Lord, save us! We are perishing!" (v. 25), and Jesus asks why they are so afraid. Tell about a storm in your own life. What did you do with your fear, and where was God in it?

After the storm, the men ask, "What kind of man is this?" (v. 27). Then a whole town begs Jesus to leave (v. 34). Why might people react so differently to him, and where are you in that picture today?
8.life: Pick one worry you are carrying this week. Each morning, bring it to Jesus in a sentence or two, as the leper and the centurion did, and tell him honestly whether you trust his power, his willingness, or both.
8.prayer: Thank Jesus that he touches, listens and carries what we cannot. Ask for honest faith, even if it is small, and pray for anyone in the group who is in a storm right now.
8.tip: Verses 21 and 22 and the pigs in verses 30 to 32 are puzzling, and the chapter does not explain them. Say so plainly, note that readers understand the burial request in more than one way, and steer back to the question of who Jesus is and how people respond to him.

9.open: Think of a meal you still remember. Who was around the table, and what made it stick with you?
questions: Before anything else, Jesus tells the paralyzed man, "Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven" (v. 2). Why might Jesus start there instead of with the thing everyone could see was wrong?
The scribes thought, "This man is blaspheming!" (v. 3), because they believed only God can forgive sins. What were they getting right, and what were they missing?
Jesus says, "It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick" (v. 12). What do you think it means to admit you need a doctor, and why is that sometimes hard?
The Pharisees asked why Jesus ate with "tax collectors and sinners" (v. 11). Who would people be surprised to see at your table, and what makes those lines feel important to us?
Jesus quotes, "I desire mercy, not sacrifice" (v. 13). Where do you see religious habits and real mercy pulling apart, in the church today or in your own life?

The woman touched His cloak, saying to herself, "If only I touch His cloak, I will be healed" (v. 21). Jesus called her "daughter" and did not leave her hidden in the crowd. What does that tell you about how He sees people on the edges?

When Jesus asked the blind men, "Do you believe that I am able to do this?" they answered, "Yes, Lord" (v. 28). If He asked you that about something in your life right now, what would you honestly say, even if the answer is that you are not sure?
Jesus saw the crowds as "harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd" (v. 36). Who around you feels that way, and what would it look like to care for them the way Jesus did?
9.life: Invite someone to share a meal or a coffee this week, ideally someone you would not normally sit down with. Come to listen, not to fix anything.
9.prayer: Thank Jesus that He sees people others pass by, including us. Ask Him for honesty about where you need healing, and for a heart that notices people the way He does.
9.tip: The healings can lead to the question of why Jesus does not heal everyone today. Do not try to answer it fully. Name it as an honest, painful question, let people say what they feel, and bring the group back to what this chapter shows about Jesus' compassion.

10.open: Think of a time you were sent out to do something you did not feel ready for, like a first day at a job or a trip on your own. What was that like?
questions: The twelve include Matthew the tax collector and Simon the Zealot, two men who would normally have been enemies, and Judas, who "betrayed Jesus" (v. 4). What does it tell you that Jesus chose such a mixed group?
Jesus tells them, "Freely you have received; freely give" (v. 8). What have you freely received that you could pass on to someone else?
The twelve are told to travel light and depend on those who welcome them (vv. 9-11). What does that kind of dependence on others look like for us, and why can it be hard?
Jesus says, "I am sending you out like sheep among wolves" (v. 16). Why do you think he is so honest about the danger instead of making the mission sound easy?

Jesus says, "Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul" (v. 28), and then reminds them that not one sparrow falls "apart from the will of your Father" (v. 29). What are you most afraid of right now, and how does this passage speak to it, or fail to?

Jesus says, "I have not come to bring peace, but a sword" (v. 34). Most readers take this to mean that loyalty to him can divide families, not that he calls for violence. Have you seen faith bring tension into a relationship? How did you handle it?

Jesus says, "Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for My sake will find it" (v. 39). Is there anything that feels like a loss in following him, and anything that has felt like a gain? Feel free to say if you are unsure.
Verse 42 promises a reward even for "a cup of cold water" given to one of Jesus' followers. What small acts of kindness have been given to you, and who might you give one to?
10.life: Pick one person this week and do one small, quiet kindness for them, like a meal, a note or a ride, without expecting anything back. Then thank God for the times someone did that for you.
10.prayer: Thank God that he knows you down to "the very hairs of your head" (v. 30). Ask him to take the fears you named tonight and give you courage to follow him one step at a time.
10.tip: Verses 34 to 39 can leave people feeling guilty if their family is not on board with their faith, or worried that loving family is wrong. Remind the group that Jesus is describing the cost some will face, not telling anyone to love their family less. Let people share without fixing it, and be gentle with anyone for whom this is painful.

11.open: When did you last wait a long time for something, and what helped you keep going?
questions: John is in prison when he asks, "Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?" (v. 3). Why might a faithful person start to wonder, and what do you make of the fact that Jesus does not scold him?

Jesus answers by pointing to what is happening: "The blind receive sight, the lame walk" (v. 5). When your hopes turn out different from what you expected, what kind of evidence actually helps you decide whether something is still real?
Jesus says, "Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me" (v. 6). What are some things that could make a person stumble over Jesus today, even a person who loves him?
Jesus asks the crowds what they went out to see in John, and says no one greater has risen (v. 11). What stands out to you about the kind of person Jesus praises here?

Jesus says people called John demon-possessed for fasting, and called him a "glutton and drunkard" for feasting (vv. 18, 19). When have you seen people find a reason to dismiss something no matter how it was offered?

Jesus warns the towns where he did most of his miracles, because "they did not repent" (v. 20). Why might people who see the most still be the slowest to change? Is there anything familiar in that for us?
Jesus thanks the Father for revealing these things to "little children" (v. 25). What does it look like to come to God that way, without needing to have everything figured out?

Jesus says, "Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest" (v. 28). What is wearing you out right now, and what would it mean to bring it to him? If that feels hard or you are not sure he will meet you there, say so honestly.
11.life: Pick one burden you have been carrying alone. Each day this week, name it to Jesus in a sentence or two and ask him for the rest he promised. If you have a doubt you have never said out loud, include that too.
11.prayer: Thank Jesus that he is "gentle and humble in heart" (v. 29). Ask him to meet anyone in the group who is weary or doubting, and to give each person rest.
11.tip: Verses 20 to 24 are a hard warning and people may want to skip past them or argue about who is judged. Name that it is serious, keep the focus on Jesus' sorrow that people did not turn to him, and then let the invitation in verses 28 to 30 carry the end of the evening. Also note that Christians differ on whether John truly doubted or asked mainly for his followers' sake, and you do not need to settle it.

12.open: When did a rule or a plan get in the way of something that mattered more, and what did you do?
questions: The Pharisees said the disciples were doing what was "unlawful on the Sabbath" (v. 2). Why do you think they cared so much about this rule, and what were they trying to protect?
Jesus quotes, "I desire mercy, not sacrifice" (v. 7). What do you think he means, and where do you see rule-keeping crowd out mercy today?
Jesus says, "it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath" (v. 12). When a rule and a real need pull in different directions, how do you decide which should give way?

Matthew describes a servant who will not break "a bruised reed" or put out "a smoldering wick" (v. 20). Where do you feel bruised or close to burning out, and what does it mean that Jesus handles people this gently?

Jesus says, "if I drive out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you" (v. 28). The crowd was astounded while the Pharisees explained it away. Why can the same event lead people to such different conclusions?

Verses 31 and 32 speak of blasphemy against the Spirit that "will not be forgiven." Christians understand this in different ways. What fears or questions does this raise for you, and what does the rest of the chapter, including the gentle servant, say to those fears?
Jesus says, "out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks" (v. 34). What do your words, especially the careless ones, tend to reveal about what is going on inside you?
Jesus says, "whoever does the will of My Father in heaven is My brother and sister and mother" (v. 50). What would it look like for our group to live like family in that sense?
12.life: This week, notice one moment when you are tempted to put a rule, a habit or an image ahead of a person who needs help. Choose mercy in that moment, and tell someone in the group how it went.
12.prayer: Thank God that Jesus is gentle with the bruised and the weary. Ask him to soften your heart toward people, to guard your words, and to make this group a place where people feel like family.
12.tip: Verses 31 and 32 may stir real fear in someone who worries they have gone too far. Say plainly that Christians understand this passage differently, then point to the context: Jesus is speaking to people who called the Spirit's work Satan's, and a person who is troubled about it is not showing the hard refusal he describes. Offer to talk privately afterward with anyone who is anxious.

13.open: What is the hardest thing you have ever tried to grow, whether a garden, a plant, a habit or a friendship?
questions: Jesus ends the first story with "He who has ears, let him hear" (v. 9). What do you think it means to really hear something, and not just listen?

Jesus says the seed on rocky ground is the person who "at once receives it with joy," but "when trouble or persecution comes because of the word, he quickly falls away" (vv. 20, 21). What did that look like then, and what does trouble look like for someone trying to follow Jesus today?
Verse 22 names "the worries of this life and the deceitfulness of wealth" as what chokes the word. Which of those two is more likely to crowd out your attention right now, and how can you tell?

Think about the four soils. Most of us have been each one at different times. Which one describes where you are this season? Be as honest as you like, including if the honest answer is that you are not sure.

In the weeds and wheat story, the owner says, "Let both grow together until the harvest" (v. 30). Why might he refuse to pull the weeds now, and what does that say about how we treat people whose faith looks different from ours?
The mustard seed is "the smallest of all seeds," yet it becomes a tree (v. 32). Where have you seen something small and easy to miss turn into something that mattered?
The man who finds the treasure sells all he has "in his joy" (v. 44). How is that different from giving something up out of duty, and what might it look like in an ordinary life?
In Nazareth the people ask, "Isn't this the carpenter's son?" and "they took offense at Him" (vv. 55, 57). Why can it be hard to take seriously someone, or something, we think we already know?
13.life: Pick one of the soils that sounded most like you this season. This week, take one small step to give the seed more room: clear a distraction, find a steady time to read Scripture, or talk with someone about what is making it hard.
13.prayer: Ask God to make your heart good soil, soft and open to what he says. Pray for anyone in the group who feels dry, worried or worn down right now.
13.tip: The parable explanations talk about fire and "weeping and gnashing of teeth" (v. 42), and Christians also disagree about why Jesus used parables at all (vv. 10 to 15). Some read them as hiding truth from hardened hearts, others as an invitation to anyone willing to ask. Say that plainly, then steer back to the questions about how we listen. Also watch the soils question: do not let anyone label another person as a type of soil, and make it easy for someone to say they are not sure.

14.open: When was the last time you needed a few minutes alone, and what did you do to get them?
questions: Herod "was afraid of the people" (v. 5) and later granted a terrible request "because of his oaths and his guests" (v. 9). Why do you think fear of looking bad can push people into doing wrong?
Herod hears about Jesus and decides, "This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead!" (v. 2). What does his reaction suggest about what was going on inside him?

When Jesus heard about John, "He withdrew by boat privately to a solitary place," but the crowds followed (v. 13). Then he "had compassion on them" (v. 14). What does this show you about Jesus when he was grieving and tired?

Jesus tells the disciples, "You give them something to eat," and they answer, "We have here only five loaves of bread and two fish" (vv. 16, 17). What is something in your life right now that feels like too little for the need in front of you?
Later Jesus "went up on the mountain by Himself to pray" (v. 23). Where do you find it hardest to make space to be with God, and what gets in the way?

Peter asks to come to Jesus on the water, but "when he saw the strength of the wind, he was afraid" (v. 30). Then Jesus "reached out His hand and took hold of Peter" (v. 31). What stands out to you about the order of those events?
Jesus asks, "why did you doubt?" (v. 31). Where do you honestly find doubt or fear rising up in your faith right now? You can answer in a sentence, or just say pass if you would rather listen.
After the wind died down, the disciples worshiped Jesus and said, "Truly You are the Son of God!" (v. 33). Why might a frightening night have led them to say that?
14.life: Pick one worry that feels bigger than what you have to give. This week, say it to God in plain words each day, and ask for one small, practical step you can take with what you do have.
14.prayer: Thank Jesus that he meets us in grief, hunger and storms. Ask him to take hold of whatever is making you afraid right now, and to help you trust him with what you have.
14.tip: Many people will hurry to call Peter a failure for sinking. Gently point out that he was the only one who stepped out, and that Jesus caught him at once. If someone shares a real doubt, thank them and resist the urge to fix it. Christians also differ on whether the feeding and the walk on water are literal events or mainly symbolic. Most read them as literal, so say that plainly in one line and keep the focus on who Jesus is.

15.open: What is a family rule or habit in your home growing up that no one ever explained, but everyone followed?
questions: The Pharisees ask why the disciples "break the tradition of the elders" (v. 2). Jesus answers by asking why they "break the command of God for the sake of your tradition" (v. 3). In your own words, what is the difference between a tradition and a command of God?
In verses 4 to 6, a religious rule let people keep their money from supporting their parents. Why do you think someone could be sincere about a rule like that and still miss the point?

Jesus quotes Isaiah: "These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me" (v. 8). When have you gone through the motions at church or in prayer while your heart was somewhere else? What was that like?

Jesus says, "A man is not defiled by what enters his mouth, but by what comes out of it" (v. 11). Then he traces it to the heart (v. 18). Why might it be easier to focus on outside behavior than on what is going on inside?
The list in verse 19 includes "false testimony, and slander" next to murder and adultery. Which item on the list do we tend to treat too lightly?

The Canaanite woman keeps asking even when Jesus is silent and then seems to refuse her (vv. 23 to 26). Her reply is "even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their master's table" (v. 27). What do you notice about her, and what do you make of Jesus's responses? It is fine to say this passage puzzles you.

Jesus says, "I have compassion for this crowd" and "I do not want to send them away hungry" (v. 32). The disciples see only a shortage (v. 33). Where do you see a need around you that feels too big for what you have?
Think about the whole chapter, from the argument over rules to the healed daughter to the fed crowd. What does it show you about what Jesus cares about most?
15.life: This week, pick one habit or rule in your faith that you keep carefully, and ask honestly whether it is helping you love God and the people near you. Then do one small, practical thing for someone in need, such as a meal, a ride or a phone call.
15.prayer: Ask God to show you what is really in your heart, and to meet you there with grace instead of shame. Pray for eyes to notice people who are overlooked, and for the persistence of the woman who kept asking.
15.tip: Verses 26 and 27 can make people uncomfortable, and the group may want to explain them away quickly. Name that Jesus's words sound harsh and that readers differ on what he meant. Then focus on what is clear: the woman's persistence and his answer, "your faith is great!" (v. 28). Also note that Christians differ on whether verses 11 to 20 set aside the Old Testament food laws or only the handwashing tradition, so keep it brief and return to the heart.

16.open: What is something you once believed about a person, a place or a job that turned out to be completely wrong?
questions: The Pharisees and Sadducees ask for "a sign from heaven" (v. 1). Jesus says they can read the sky but not "the signs of the times" (v. 3). Why do you think people can see plenty of evidence and still want more proof?

The disciples hear "Beware of the leaven" and think Jesus is talking about forgotten bread (vv. 6-7). Jesus asks, "Do you still not understand?" (v. 9). When have you missed the point of something because you were worried about something smaller?

Jesus asks, "Who do people say the Son of Man is?" and then turns the question to the disciples themselves (vv. 13, 15). How would you answer the first question today, and how would you honestly answer the second?

Peter says, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God" (v. 16). Jesus says this was not revealed "by flesh and blood, but by My Father in heaven" (v. 17). What do you think it means that faith is something given and not only figured out? How does that sit with you?

In verse 18 Jesus says, "on this rock I will build My church." Christians read "this rock" in different ways, as Peter, as his confession, or as Jesus himself. Whichever reading you lean toward, what does it tell us about what the church is built on?

Within minutes of his great confession, Peter hears "Get behind Me, Satan!" (v. 23). Peter was trying to protect Jesus from suffering. Where do we try to steer God away from a hard road because we mean well?
Jesus says, "If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me" (v. 24). What does that look like in an ordinary week, and what makes it hard?

Jesus asks, "What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, yet forfeits his soul?" (v. 26). What do you find yourself chasing that may not be worth what it costs? If you feel unsure about all this, what is the hardest part for you to believe or accept?
16.life: Jesus asked his disciples who they said he was. This week, write your honest answer in a few sentences, doubts included. Then pick one small way you are tempted to hold on to your own life, such as your schedule, image or comfort, and offer it to God.
16.prayer: Thank Jesus for asking us directly who he is and for being patient with slow learners like Peter. Ask for honest faith and for the courage to follow him even when it costs something.
16.tip: Verses 18 and 19 can pull the whole evening into a debate about Peter and the papacy. Say in one line that Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christians read these verses differently, then bring the group back to Peter's confession in verse 16 and Jesus' question to each person.

17.open: Have you ever been somewhere so good you didn't want to leave, like a trip, a concert or a family gathering? What made it hard to come home?
questions: In verse 2 Jesus "was transfigured before them" and "His face shone like the sun." What do you think the three disciples saw in that moment that they had not seen before?
Peter says, "it is good for us to be here," and offers to build three shelters (v. 4). What moments in your own life have you wanted to hold onto, and what was it like to come back down from them?

The voice from the cloud says, "Listen to Him!" (v. 5). Moses and Elijah were great figures in Israel's story, yet in the end only Jesus remains (v. 8). What might that have meant to the disciples then?
The disciples "fell facedown in terror," and Jesus touched them and said, "Do not be afraid" (vv. 6-7). What do you notice about how Jesus treats them in their fear?
Right after the mountain, the disciples meet a father pleading, "Lord, have mercy on my son" (v. 15). Why do you think Matthew puts a glorious mountaintop next to such a painful scene?
Jesus says faith "the size of a mustard seed" is enough (v. 20). If your faith feels small or shaky right now, what would you honestly say about where it stands? There are no wrong answers here.

Jesus tells them plainly that he will be killed and raised, and the disciples are "deeply grieved" (v. 23). Why might they have heard the death more than the rising? When have you heard the hard part of a promise louder than the hopeful part?

Jesus says the sons are exempt from the tax, yet he pays so "that we may not offend them" (v. 27). Where might you have every right to something and still choose to give it up for someone else's sake?
17.life: Peter wanted to stay on the mountain, but Jesus led them back down to people in need. This week, take ten quiet minutes to simply "listen to Him" by reading a short passage from the Gospels. Then look for one person you can help or encourage.
17.prayer: Thank God that Jesus is the beloved Son and that we are told to listen to him. Ask for ears to hear him, and for trust when your faith feels small.
17.tip: Verse 20 can leave people feeling guilty, as if their faith is not enough. Point out that Jesus speaks of a mustard seed, the smallest amount, and that the father in the story came with nothing but his need. Keep the focus on Jesus' power, not on measuring anyone's faith. Also, the fish and coin in verse 27 may spark debate about whether it is literal, so a quick note that the story is told simply is enough before moving on.

18.open: Think of a time someone owed you something small, like money, a favor or an apology. How did you handle it?
questions: The disciples asked, "Who then is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?" (v. 1). Why do you think people, even good people, keep asking that kind of question?
Jesus says we must "change and become like little children" (v. 3). A child had no status in that world. What do you think Jesus wants us to let go of?
Jesus warns against causing "one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble" (v. 6). Who are the people in your life who are easily hurt or easily led, and how can we look out for them?
Verses 8 and 9 sound extreme, and most readers take them as deliberate exaggeration. What is one habit or influence you would take seriously enough to deal with firmly?

In the story of the lost sheep, the shepherd goes out to "search for the one that is lost" (v. 12). If you have ever drifted from God or from a group, what was it like, or what do you think it would have taken for someone to find you?
Jesus says to go "privately" first when someone wrongs you (v. 15). Why is that so hard to do? What usually happens instead?
Peter asks how often to forgive, and Jesus answers "seventy-seven times" (v. 22). What do you think Jesus means by that, and where do you find it hardest to keep forgiving?

The king asks, "Shouldn't you have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had on you?" (v. 33). Christians read the harsh ending differently, some seeing forgiveness actually withdrawn and others a warning that real forgiveness changes us. What do you make of it, and what questions does it leave you with?
18.life: Think of one person you have been holding something against. This week, do one concrete step: pray for them by name each day, or take the first step toward a private, kind conversation if it is safe and wise to do so.
18.prayer: Thank God for forgiving a debt we could never repay. Ask for a humble heart, eyes for the overlooked, and the strength to let go of what someone owes you.
18.tip: The ending of the parable and the steps in verses 15 to 17 can bring up painful stories, including abuse or deep hurt. Say clearly that Jesus is not asking anyone to stay in danger or pretend nothing happened, and that forgiving is not the same as trusting again. On the ending of the parable, note once that Christians read it differently, and keep the focus on the mercy the servant received.

19.open: What is something you have held onto for years that you probably could have let go of sooner?
questions: The Pharisees "tested" Jesus with a debated question about divorce (v. 3). Instead of picking a side, Jesus goes back to the beginning. Why might he do that, and what does it show about how he reads Scripture?

Jesus says, "what God has joined together, let man not separate" (v. 6). What does that tell us about how God sees marriage? How might this land differently for someone who is married, single, or divorced?

Jesus says Moses allowed divorce "because of your hardness of heart" (v. 8). What do you think he means, and how do we hold high ideals about marriage together with real compassion for people whose marriages have broken?

The disciples are the ones who are rattled by what Jesus said, and he replies, "Not everyone can accept this word" (v. 11). Is there anything in this chapter you find hard to accept or are unsure about? Be as honest as you like.

The disciples scold the people bringing children, but Jesus says, "Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them!" (v. 14). Who do we tend to push to the edges of church or community, and what would it look like to welcome them?

The young man asks, "What do I still lack?" (v. 20), and then "he went away in sorrow, because he had great wealth" (v. 22). What do you think he was really holding onto, and what do you notice about how Jesus treats him?

The disciples ask, "Who then can be saved?" and Jesus answers, "With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible" (vv. 25-26). What does this say about whether we can earn our way to God, and how does it help when the call to follow Jesus feels too big?
19.life: Pick one thing you own or rely on, such as money, a title, a routine or a comfort, and hold it loosely this week. Ask God honestly what place it has in your life, and do one small act of generosity with it.
19.prayer: Thank God that what we cannot do, he can. Ask for honesty about what we hold tightly, and pray for anyone in the group whose marriage or family is hurting.
19.tip: Verses 3 to 9 will be personal for anyone who has been through divorce, and Christians disagree about the exception in verse 9: many Protestants read it as allowing remarriage after adultery, Catholic teaching reads it more narrowly, and Orthodox churches allow remarriage in some cases. Say that plainly, don't try to settle it tonight, and remind the group that most churches agree this teaching never requires anyone to stay where they are being harmed. Keep the tone gentle and bring the discussion back to Jesus' welcome and his words in verse 26.

20.open: When did you last get something you felt you didn't earn, like a free upgrade, a kind gift or a second chance?
questions: The landowner keeps going back to the marketplace, even at the eleventh hour. The last workers say, "Because no one has hired us" (v. 7). What does this tell us about the kind of master Jesus is describing?
The early workers "began to grumble against the landowner" (v. 11), even though they got exactly what they agreed to. Why does their pay feel unfair to them? When have you felt something like that?
The landowner asks, "Or are you envious because I am generous?" (v. 15). Where in life do you find it hardest to be glad when someone else is treated well?

Christians read the equal wage differently. Some see it as salvation given equally to all, and others think there is still room for different rewards. How does each reading shape the way you hear the story?

Right after Jesus says he will be "mocked and flogged and crucified" (v. 19), the mother of James and John asks for the best seats in his kingdom (v. 21). Why do you think she and her sons were not hearing what he said? When have you heard only what you hoped to hear?

Jesus says, "whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant" (v. 26). What does greatness look like in our culture, and what would it look like if we lived this verse at home, at work or at church?
Verse 28 says the Son of Man came "to give His life as a ransom for many." What does it mean to you that Jesus describes his own life as the one who serves us, not the one who is served?

The two blind men keep shouting when the crowd tells them to be quiet, and Jesus asks, "What do you want Me to do for you?" (v. 32). If Jesus asked you that today, what would you honestly say, even if you are unsure he will answer?
20.life: This week, quietly do one act of service for someone who cannot repay you and will not know it was you, or celebrate out loud when someone else gets a good thing you wanted.
20.prayer: Thank God for being generous beyond what we deserve. Ask him to loosen envy and the need to compare, and to give each person the courage to say honestly what they want him to do for them.
20.tip: The vineyard story can sound unfair, and someone may say so. Let them. Ask the group why it feels that way, then point to verse 15. Don't rush to settle whether the wage means salvation or reward, since Christians differ. Keep the focus on the landowner's generosity.

22.open: Tell about a time you were invited to something you almost didn't go to. What made you say yes or no?
questions: In the story, the invited guests "paid no attention and went away, one to his field, another to his business" (v. 5). What ordinary things can crowd out an invitation from God in our lives?
The king sends servants out to the crossroads to gather "everyone they could find, both evil and good" (v. 10). What does that tell us about who is welcome at God's table?
In verses 11 to 13 a guest turns up without wedding clothes and is thrown out. That is a hard scene to read. What troubles you about it, and what do you think Jesus wants us to see?

The Pharisees and Herodians open with flattery, then ask a trap question about taxes (vv. 16, 17). Jesus answers, "Give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's" (v. 21). What do you think belongs to God in your own life?

Jesus tells the Sadducees, "You are mistaken because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God" (v. 29). Where do you find yourself unsure about life after death, and what questions do you carry about it?

Jesus says, "Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind" (v. 37). Which of those three, heart, soul or mind, comes most easily to you, and which is harder?
The second commandment is "Love your neighbor as yourself" (v. 39). Who is a neighbor you find hard to love right now, and what would loving them look like in a small, real way?
Four groups bring Jesus questions in this chapter, some honest and some meant to trap him. If you could ask Jesus one honest question tonight, even a doubtful one, what would it be?
22.life: Pick one person this week who is hard to love, and do one small, practical thing for them. Before you do it, say the two great commandments in verses 37 to 39 slowly to yourself.
22.prayer: Thank God for inviting us to his table, whoever we are. Ask for a heart that answers that invitation and grows in love for God and for the people around us.
22.tip: The man without wedding clothes (vv. 11 to 13) will likely stir strong reactions, since it seems to clash with the welcome in verse 10. Say plainly that Christians differ on what the clothes mean, some seeing a gift from God and others a changed life, and many both. Then steer back to the main point: the invitation is real, and it calls for a response.

23.open: When you were a kid, what did you do to look like you had cleaned your room when you really hadn't?
questions: Jesus says of the scribes and Pharisees that "they do not practice what they preach" (v. 3). Why do you think it is so easy to say one thing and live another?
Verse 4 says they "tie up heavy, burdensome loads" for others but will not lift a finger to help. What does it look like today when religion becomes a burden on people instead of help?
Jesus says, "All their deeds are done for men to see" (v. 5). Where do you notice the pull to be seen as good, whether at church, at work or online?
In verse 11 Jesus says, "The greatest among you shall be your servant." Who has shown you what that looks like, and what did they do?

In verse 23 Jesus names "justice, mercy, and faithfulness" as the weightier matters, and says the small rules should not be neglected either. Why might it be tempting to focus on easy, measurable things and skip the harder ones?

Jesus describes people who "appear to be righteous" outside but are full of hypocrisy inside (v. 28). Without naming anyone else, what is one thing in your own life that looks tidier from the outside than it is on the inside?

The chapter ends with Jesus saying, "how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings" (v. 37). How does this change the way you hear the strong words earlier in the chapter?
If you are not sure what you believe about God, or you find this chapter hard to read, what stands out to you, and what questions does it raise?
23.life: This week, pick one quiet act of service that no one will see or thank you for, and do it. Afterwards, notice honestly how it felt, and tell God about it.
23.prayer: Ask God to show you where you are more concerned with looking good than being good, and to meet you there with mercy. Thank him that Jesus longs to gather us in, not push us away.
23.tip: The harsh words can sound like an attack on Jewish people as a whole, and they have been misused that way. Remind the group that Jesus was a Jew speaking to fellow Jews about specific leaders, and that the chapter ends in grief. Steer the group to look at their own hearts rather than pointing at others. The judgment at the end is read in different ways by Christians, so don't try to settle it tonight.

24.open: Have you ever been waiting for someone to arrive, like a guest, a delivery or a late friend, and had no idea when they would show up? What did you do while you waited?
questions: The disciples point proudly to the temple buildings, and Jesus says "not one stone here will be left on another" (v. 2). What do you think went through their minds? What impressive thing today do people count on to last?

Jesus begins his answer with "See to it that no one deceives you" (v. 4). Why do you think he starts there rather than with dates or signs? Where do you see people trying to convince others that they have the answers about the end?

Jesus says wars, famines and earthquakes are "the beginning of birth pains" (v. 8). What does that picture of birth pains tell you about how to read bad news in the world? How do you usually react to it?
Verse 12 says "the love of most will grow cold," and verse 13 says "the one who perseveres to the end will be saved." What tends to cool your own love or energy for faith? What helps you keep going?

Verse 34 says "this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened." Christians read this differently: some think it points to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, others to a later generation or something broader. What do you make of it, and what do all of those readings still agree on?

Verse 36 says "No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father." What do you notice about Jesus saying this about himself? How does it affect the urge to predict dates?

Jesus says the end will come in ordinary life, as in the days of Noah when people were "eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage" (v. 38). What would it look like to be ready without living in panic or ignoring daily life?

The faithful servant is the one "doing so" when the master returns, giving the household "their food at the proper time" (vv. 45, 46). What is one small, steady thing you could be doing for the people around you? If this chapter leaves you anxious, unsure or doubtful, what part troubles you most?
24.life: Pick one ordinary, faithful act of care for someone in your household, church or neighborhood, like a meal, a call or a ride, and do it each day this week. Treat it as your way of keeping watch.
24.prayer: Ask God for a steady heart that is neither frightened nor careless about what is coming. Pray for the grace to love others faithfully while we wait, and for anyone in the group who feels anxious or unsure.
24.tip: This chapter can pull a group into timelines and arguments about the end. Say up front that Christians read parts of it differently, and keep steering back to what everyone can agree on: do not be deceived, do not be alarmed, and stay faithful. Be gentle with anyone who is anxious about the hard verses.

25.open: Have you ever been waiting on someone who was really late, and what did you do to pass the time?
questions: The five wise virgins brought extra oil, and the foolish ones "did not take along any extra oil" (v. 3). What do you think it looks like to be ready for a long wait rather than a short one?
The story never says what the oil stands for. Readers have suggested faith, good deeds or God's Spirit. What do you think it might mean, and why?

The bridegroom says, "I do not know you" (v. 12), and Jesus ends with, "keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour" (v. 13). How does this verse land with you: as a warning, an invitation, or something else?

A talent was a huge sum of money. The master gives it "each according to his own ability" (v. 15). What has God put in your hands, such as time, skills, money or relationships, that you could put to work?

The third servant says, "I was afraid and went out and hid your talent in the ground" (v. 25). When has fear kept you from doing something good? What did the servant believe about his master, and how might that have shaped what he did?
The master tells the faithful servants, "Enter into the joy of your master!" (v. 21). What do you picture when you hear that? How is it different from a reward for work done?

The king says, "whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me" (v. 40). Who are the people in your town or church who are easy to overlook, and what is one small thing someone could do for them?

Verses 41 to 46 are hard to read, and Christians have understood the final outcome differently. If you find this part troubling, or you are not sure what you believe about it, what is it that bothers you most?
25.life: Pick one person in need that you know of, whether hungry, lonely, sick or new in town, and do one small, practical thing for them this week. Then tell someone in the group how it went.
25.prayer: Ask God for a heart that stays ready and awake while waiting. Pray for the courage to use what he has given you instead of hiding it, and for eyes to see the people he wants you to notice.
25.tip: The last third of the chapter can push a group toward either fear or a debate about hell. Say plainly that Christians read verses 41 to 46 differently, then bring the group back to what all the stories share: stay ready, use what you have been given, and care for people. Also keep an eye out for anyone who hears verse 40 as a list of things they have failed to do. Remind them the chapter begins and ends with the king's welcome and not his scorn.

26.open: Think of a time you let a friend down when it counted. What helped you make it right, or what do you wish had been different?
questions: The disciples saw the perfume and asked, "Why this waste?" (v. 8). Jesus called it "a beautiful deed" (v. 10). When has something done out of love looked wasteful to others? What do you think made it beautiful to Jesus?
Judas asked, "What are you willing to give me if I hand Him over to you?" (v. 15). What do you think was going on in him? Why might someone close to Jesus end up here?
When Jesus said one of them would betray him, each disciple asked, "Surely not I, Lord?" (v. 22). Why do you think they all wondered about themselves instead of pointing at someone else?

Jesus said of the cup, "This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins" (v. 28). What does it mean to you that he gave this meal to his friends right before they failed him?

In Gethsemane Jesus prayed, "My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me. Yet not as I will, but as You will" (v. 39). What does it say to you that Jesus asked to be spared and still said yes? Have you ever prayed a prayer like that, or found it hard to?
Jesus said, "the spirit is willing, but the body is weak" (v. 41), as his friends fell asleep. Where do you see that gap in your own life, between what you want to do and what you actually do?

Peter said, "Even if I have to die with You, I will never deny You" (v. 35), and hours later said, "I do not know the man!" (v. 72). What do you think separates who we mean to be from who we are under pressure?
Peter "went outside and wept bitterly" (v. 75). If you are honest, do you tend to hide when you fail, or come back? What would make coming back easier?
26.life: Pick one moment this week when you feel pressure to stay quiet about your faith or go along with the crowd. Before it comes, ask God for help. Afterward, whether you did well or badly, tell him about it plainly and without hiding.
26.prayer: Thank Jesus for going to the cross willingly for people who would fail him. Ask for honesty about where you are weak, and for the courage to come back to him after you fall.
26.tip: Judas and Peter both fail badly, and some people in the group may feel afraid they are more like one than the other. Keep the focus on what the chapter shows: Jesus knows all of it ahead of time and still shares the meal. Also, Christians differ on what Jesus meant by "this is My body" (v. 26), some holding that the bread and wine truly carry his body and blood and others that they are a symbol and a way of remembering him. Name that in a sentence and move on, so the meal's meaning is not lost in the argument.

27.open: Think of a time you were blamed for something you didn't do, or went along with a group when you wish you hadn't. What was that like?
questions: Pilate knew "it was out of envy that they had handed Jesus over to him" (v. 18), and he asked, "What evil has He done?" (v. 23). Why do you think he still gave in?
Pilate washed his hands and said, "I am innocent of this man's blood" (v. 24). Where do people today try to wash their hands of something they helped allow to happen?

The crowd cried, "His blood be on us and on our children!" (v. 25). This verse was later twisted to blame all Jewish people, and most churches firmly reject that reading. Why is it important to read a verse like this carefully and with humility?
Jesus "gave no answer" to the charges (v. 14), and the soldiers mocked him with "Hail, King of the Jews!" (v. 29). What strikes you about a king who takes this without fighting back?
The passersby and leaders said, "He saved others, but He cannot save Himself" (v. 42). In what way might those words be true in a way they didn't mean?

Jesus cried, "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" (v. 46). Christians read this in different ways. Some hear real abandonment, some hear the whole psalm it comes from, which ends in trust, and many hear both. What do you hear in it, and what do you do when God feels far away?
The officer and the soldiers said, "Truly this was the Son of God" (v. 54). Why might it matter that these words came from outsiders at the foot of the cross?
Many women watched "from a distance" (v. 55), and Joseph gave his own new tomb (v. 60). What can we learn from people who couldn't fix anything but still showed up?
27.life: This week, notice one moment when you could quietly go along with the crowd, whether in a conversation, a group chat or at work. Choose one small, kind way to speak up or step away, and tell someone from the group how it went.
27.prayer: Thank Jesus for going to the cross for us, and ask him to help you see him clearly. Pray for anyone who feels forsaken tonight, and for courage to stand with people who are treated unfairly.
27.tip: Verse 25 needs a calm, clear word from you early on. Say plainly that it has been used to blame Jewish people, that most churches reject that reading, and that every person in the chapter, including us, is part of the story. Also, if the cry in verse 46 raises hard feelings, let people say so honestly without rushing to tidy it up.

28.open: What is the best surprise you have ever received, either one you gave or one that was given to you?
questions: The angel tells the women, "Do not be afraid" (v. 5), yet verse 8 says they left "in fear and great joy." Why might fear and joy show up together when something this big happens?
The angel says, "He is not here; He has risen, just as He said!" (v. 6). What do you think it meant for these women that Jesus had said it would happen and then it did?
In verse 10 Jesus calls the disciples "My brothers," even though they had run away from him. What does that tell you about how Jesus treats people who have failed him?
The women were the first to be sent with the news, in a time when their word was often not taken seriously. What stands out to you about who Jesus chooses to trust with this message?

The chief priests paid the guards "a large sum of money" to tell a different story (v. 12). Why do you think people work so hard to explain away something they cannot control? Where do you see that today?
Verse 17 says, "they worshiped Him, but some doubted." Where are you right now: worshiping, doubting, or somewhere in between? You can answer in your own words, and honest answers are welcome here.

Jesus says, "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me" (v. 18) before he sends them out. How might knowing that change the way someone goes about sharing their faith or living it out?
Jesus ends with "I am with you always, even to the end of the age" (v. 20). When have you most needed to hear that, and what would it look like to lean on it this week?
28.life: Jesus' last words in Matthew are a promise to be with us always. This week, pick one ordinary moment each day, like a commute or a meal, to pause and remember that promise. If you doubt, tell God so plainly. Then reach out to one person who might need encouragement and tell them how you are doing.
28.prayer: Thank Jesus for being alive and for staying with us. Ask him to meet the worship and the doubts in this room, and to give each person courage for the next step he is asking of them.
28.tip: Verse 17 may bring out people's doubts, and some may feel embarrassed to speak. Point out that Matthew records the doubt openly, even with Jesus standing in front of them, and that Jesus still stays and speaks to them. Let people answer at their own pace, and do not rush to fix anyone's questions. If the group touches on whether the resurrection was literal and bodily, say plainly that most Christians read it that way while some read it less literally, then return to the chapter.
